summary.text: A chi-squared test is a hypothesis test used on contingency tables when sample sizes are large, mainly to examine whether two categorical variables are independent.
Pearson's version asks whether there is a statistically significant difference between the expected frequencies and the observed frequencies in one or more categories.
Pearson published his paper on the test in 1900, a foundation of modern statistics, and Fisher's exact test is used instead for smaller samples.

items.prompt: A survey tallies how many people live in each of several neighborhoods and hold each of several job types. What can a chi-squared test of that table tell us?

options.label: Whether average income differs between neighborhoods
Whether job type and neighborhood are independent of each other
Which neighborhood has the most people
The exact chance that the null hypothesis is true

items.explain: The test is primarily used to examine whether two categorical variables, the two dimensions of a contingency table, are independent.

items.prompt: A table of counts has only a handful of observations in total. What is the recommended alternative to the chi-squared test?

options.label: Pearson's chi-squared test, since size makes no difference
Dropping the null hypothesis
Fisher's exact test, used for smaller samples
Splitting categories to build a bigger table

items.explain: The chi-squared test is for contingency tables with large samples; for smaller sample sizes Fisher's exact test is used instead.

items.prompt: An analyst applies Yates's continuity correction to a chi-squared calculation. What happens to the p-value?

options.label: It falls, because a correction strengthens the evidence
It is unchanged; only the look of the formula changes
It falls to exactly zero
It rises, because the chi-squared value shrinks

items.explain: The correction subtracts 0.5 from each absolute difference, which reduces the chi-squared value and thus increases its p-value.

options.label: A test of goodness of fit
A test of whether two means are equal
A way to avoid contingency tables

items.explain: Pearson's paper investigated a test of goodness of fit.

items.prompt: Planners decide in advance how many residents to sample in each of four neighborhoods, then compare the shares of blue-collar, white-collar and no-collar workers across them. What question are they testing?

options.label: Independence, since residents are picked at random
Homogeneity: whether the proportions are the same in each neighborhood
Goodness of fit to a normal distribution

items.prompt: In a standard chi-squared test, the classes truly do not differ in the population. What distribution does the computed statistic follow?

options.label: A normal bell curve centered on zero
A uniform spread over all possible values
A χ² distribution
A distribution chosen by the researcher's alpha

items.explain: If the null hypothesis of no differences between the classes is true, the test statistic computed from the observations follows a χ² frequency distribution.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: A chi-squared test, also written χ² test, is a hypothesis test used to analyse contingency tables when the samples are large. Its main job is to check whether two categorical variables, the two dimensions of such a table, are independent. When the samples are smaller, Fisher's exact test is used in its place.

paragraphs.heading: Observed against expected
paragraphs.text: One version, Pearson's chi-squared test, asks whether the frequencies you observe differ significantly from the frequencies you would expect, in one or more categories of the table. The observations are sorted into classes that do not overlap. If the null hypothesis holds, meaning the classes do not differ in the population, the statistic follows a χ² distribution. The whole aim is to judge how likely the observed frequencies would be if that null hypothesis were true.

paragraphs.heading: An approximation with a fix
paragraphs.text: In many cases the statistic only approaches the χ² distribution, getting closer and closer as sample sizes grow. Reading a table of counts with the continuous χ² distribution rests on an assumption that is not quite correct and brings in some error. To shrink that error in 2 × 2 tables, Frank Yates proposed a correction for continuity: take 0.5 off the size of the gap between every observed count and its expected count. This lowers the chi-squared value and so raises its p-value.

paragraphs.heading: How it began
paragraphs.text: In the 19th century, statistical methods were used mainly on biological data, and researchers customarily assumed their observations followed a normal distribution. Near the end of that century, Karl Pearson noticed significant skewness in some biological observations. In 1900 he published a paper on the χ² test, studying a test of goodness of fit, and that paper is seen as one of the foundations of modern statistics. One of his conclusions about an approximation stirred controversy that was not settled until Fisher's papers of 1922 and 1924.

paragraphs.heading: Checking a factory's variance
paragraphs.text: The χ² distribution can also test the variance of a normally distributed population. Picture a manufacturing process that has run steadily for a long time, so its variance is known almost without error. A new variant of the process is tried, giving a small sample of n items. The test statistic T squares each item's deviation from the sample mean, adds these up, and divides by the variance being tested, and T then follows the chi-squared distribution having n − 1 degrees of freedom. With a sample of 21, the acceptance region for T at a 5% significance level runs from 9.59 to 34.17.

paragraphs.heading: Codes and genes
paragraphs.text: The test turns up far from the classroom. Code breakers use it to compare the distribution of plaintext with that of ciphertext that may have been decrypted, and the lowest value of the test signals that decryption very probably worked. In bioinformatics it compares properties of genes, such as mutation rate, across categories like disease genes and essential genes.
